title: std::unique_ptr and Ownership
objectives: Explain unique_ptr as RAII specialised for memory: exclusive ownership, deletion in the destructor, zero overhead
Use make_unique, reset, release and get correctly, and state what each does to ownership
Transfer ownership with std::move and describe the exact state of a moved-from unique_ptr
Design APIs around unique_ptr: sink parameters, factory returns, and custom deleters for non-memory resources
motivation: After RAII, the remaining heap bugs come from ownership ambiguity, two pointers, one object, no agreement about who deletes. std::unique_ptr makes ownership a *type-level fact*: exactly one pointer owns the object, copying is a compile error, moving hands it off, and the destructor deletes with zero size or speed overhead. It is the default smart pointer in modern C++ and the basis of every ownership discussion in code review.

blocks.md: **Ownership** answers one question: who is responsible for deleting this object? With raw pointers the answer lives in comments and conventions, which is why the double-delete and leak bugs from earlier lessons exist. `std::unique_ptr<T>` encodes the answer in the type: it holds a raw T* and deletes the object in its own destructor, and it is **movable but not copyable**, so there can only ever be one unique_ptr to an object. With the default deleter, `sizeof(std::unique_ptr<T>)` equals `sizeof(T*)` and deleting is a plain destructor call, this is the famous **zero-overhead** property. You get RAII cleanup and compile-time ownership checking for the price of nothing at runtime.

rows: destroy the current object now (optionally take a new one)
surrender ownership; returns the raw pointer and nulls p, caller must delete
observe the raw pointer without any ownership change
transfer ownership to q; p becomes null

blocks.md: `std::make_unique<T>(args...)` (C++14) allocates and constructs in one expression and is the preferred spelling: no naked new, and it composes safely with other function arguments in a way that two-step `unique_ptr<T>(new T)` does not. Ownership moves with `std::move`, after which the source is **null**, that is the entire moved-from contract for unique_ptr: valid, empty, safe to assign or reset, unsafe to dereference.

blocks.caption: std::move is a hand-off: after it, the source owns nothing.

blocks.title: unique_ptr from raw pointer does not copy-initialise
blocks.md: `std::unique_ptr<Fill> f = new Fill(3);` does **not** compile: the pointer constructor is explicit, deliberately blocking implicit ownership grabs. Write `std::make_unique<Fill>(3)` or use braces: `std::unique_ptr<Fill> f{new Fill(3)};`.

items: **Sink parameter** `void risk(std::unique_ptr<Fill> f)` - the callee takes ownership; callers must spell `std::move`, making the hand-off visible at the call site.
**Factory return** `std::unique_ptr<Fill> make_fill()` - ownership moves out to the caller; the compiler elides or moves, never copies.
**Observe**, pass `Fill*` (from `.get()`) or `Fill&`; never `const std::unique_ptr<Fill>&`, which adds nothing over a plain pointer but restricts callers.
**Arrays** - `std::unique_ptr<T[]>` (created by `std::make_unique<T[]>(n)`) calls delete[]; regular unique_ptr<T> calls delete. The pairing rule is enforced by the type.
**In containers** - `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Order>>` owns a collection of exclusively-owned objects; sorting and erasing move pointers around, never the objects.

blocks.md: The second template parameter is a deleter, anything callable taking T*. This turns unique_ptr into a general resource wrapper: file handles closed with fclose, C sessions freed with a library-specific function, connection descriptors closed. If the deleter is stateless (a lambda with no captures, or a function pointer to a function), the unique_ptr remains pointer-sized because the deleter needs no storage.

blocks.caption: A stateless-lambda deleter keeps the wrapper pointer-sized.

blocks.md: `unique_ptr` is not a convenience, it is a *proof technique* encoded in the type system. Owning the object through a move-only type means ownership has a single, statically-checkable path from construction to destruction. When a `unique_ptr` compiles, you have proven there is exactly one owner at every program point; leaks and double-frees stop being runtime events and become compile errors in someone else's code. That is the whole pitch, and it is why modern style guides say "no naked `new`".

blocks.caption: Ownership as proof: one owner at all times, destruction at scope exit, copy deleted.

blocks.md: The three habits that make this second nature. **Factory functions return by value**, the compiler turns it into a move (or elides it entirely); returning a raw pointer from a factory is how ownership ambiguity starts. **`make_unique` over `new`**, one allocation instead of two, and immune to the leak-on-exception window between `new` and the constructor of the smart pointer. **Parameters say what they mean**: a function taking `unique_ptr<T>` by value *consumes* the object; taking `T&` merely borrows; taking `T*` is a maybe-null borrow. Reading a signature should tell you the ownership story without a comment.

blocks.title: The silent killer: unique_ptr across threads
blocks.md: Passing a `unique_ptr` to another thread by reference-to-local (or capturing it by reference in a lambda) destroys the single-owner proof, two threads now race on the same owning pointer. The correct moves: pass by value (the move transfers ownership into the receiving thread), or share deliberately with `shared_ptr` (and accept its atomic-refcount cost). A data race on ownership is the worst kind because it often *works* in tests.

blocks.caption: After the move, one stack slot owns the heap object and the other is null: ownership is visible in memory, not in comments.

guidedExercise.prompt: Build a two-stage pipeline for an order object: `load_order()` returns `std::unique_ptr<Order>`; `risk_stage(std::unique_ptr<Order> o)` is a sink that takes ownership and destroys the object when it returns. Print who owns the order at each stage, move it through the pipeline, and prove at the end that main no longer owns it. Predict the exact output before running.
hints: A function taking unique_ptr *by value* is a sink: the caller must std::move.
After passing to the sink, main's unique_ptr is in the moved-from state, what is that state?
The sink's parameter is destroyed when the function returns, exactly like any automatic object.
(a) Only the acquisition line changes; delete disappears.
(b) 'Valid but null', classify assign, reset, dereference, delete.
(c) release() hands ownership to the caller, who then owns the delete obligation.

commonMistakes: Writing `std::unique_ptr<Fill> f = new Fill(3);` - the pointer constructor is explicit, so this fails to compile; use make_unique.
Dereferencing a moved-from unique_ptr: it is valid but null, assign or reset it, never read through it.
Keeping the result of release() around without deleting it: release hands the delete obligation to you, which reintroduces the leak.
Using unique_ptr for objects that genuinely need multiple owners, copying is correctly rejected; the fix is shared_ptr (next lesson), not const references to unique_ptr.
Forgetting that unique_ptr<T> and unique_ptr<T[]> use different deleters: an array in a plain unique_ptr<T> is a delete/delete[] mismatch made at compile time.
realWorldApplication: Pipeline architectures pass work objects through stages exactly once; unique_ptr makes each hand-off an explicit std::move at the call site, so ownership is auditable by reading the code and double-ownership is a compile error rather than a production incident.
quantFinanceApplication: An order object is created by the strategy thread, moved to the risk stage, then moved to the gateway, each stage owning it exclusively. std::unique_ptr<Order> documents and enforces the single-owner pipeline with zero runtime cost, which matters when a million orders flow per second.
summary: unique_ptr<T> = RAII for memory with exclusive ownership: deletes in its destructor, movable, not copyable, pointer-sized with the default deleter.
reset destroys now, release surrenders ownership (caller must delete), get observes, std::move transfers, and the source ends up null.
A moved-from unique_ptr is valid but null: assign, reset or destroy it; never dereference it.
make_unique is the preferred creation form: no naked new and exception-safe argument evaluation.
API design: pass by value to sink (ownership in), return from factories (ownership out), pass raw pointers or references to observe.

quiz.explanation: make_unique constructs S ('make'). The move leaves p null (true -> 1) and q owning (q != nullptr -> 1), so '11' prints. q.reset() destroys S immediately ('kill'), then 'end' prints.

release() surrenders ownership without destroying: p becomes null ('1' prints), the object is still alive, and the manual `delete raw` runs the destructor ('~S'). Had delete been forgotten, this would be a leak.

options: Copying is too slow to be practical
Exclusive ownership: two owning pointers to one object would delete it twice, exactly the double-free bug
It is a legacy design choice; copying is allowed since C++17
Because the standard library could not overload operator= correctly
quiz.explanation: Copy operations are deleted so the double-ownership/double-delete bug is a compile error instead of runtime UB. Ownership moves instead, the source ends up null.

quiz.prompt: Which are valid ways to bring a std::unique_ptr<T> into existence (T has an int ctor)?
quiz.explanation: make_unique, brace (direct) initialisation from a raw pointer, and a null unique_ptr followed by reset are all valid. Copy-initialisation from a raw pointer is not: the pointer constructor is explicit.

quiz.prompt: With the default deleter, how does sizeof(std::unique_ptr<T>) compare to sizeof(T*)?
options: Twice as large, it also stores a reference count
The same size, zero-overhead: a raw pointer plus a stateless deleter
Larger by the size of a control block pointer
It depends on T's alignment in all cases
quiz.explanation: unique_ptr with the default (stateless) deleter is exactly pointer-sized; access costs a plain pointer dereference with no reference counting. This is the zero-overhead property that makes it the default smart pointer.

quiz.prompt: A function signature reads `void archive(std::unique_ptr<Report> r)`. What does this signature communicate to callers, and what must callers do at the call site?
quiz.modelAnswer: It is a sink: archive takes ownership of the Report and will destroy it. Callers must transfer ownership explicitly with std::move (the argument is an lvalue), e.g. archive(std::move(my_report)), and lose access to it afterwards.
quiz.explanation: Passing unique_ptr by value means the callee owns the object; the required std::move at the call site makes the ownership hand-off visible in the code rather than hidden in a comment.

flashcards.front: What does std::unique_ptr guarantee, and at what runtime cost?
flashcards.back: Exclusive ownership with deletion in its destructor; movable, not copyable. Zero overhead: pointer-sized and no indirection with the default deleter.
reset(): destroy the owned object now. release(): give up ownership, return the raw pointer (caller must delete). get(): observe the raw pointer without touching ownership.

flashcards.front: What is the state of a moved-from unique_ptr?
flashcards.back: Valid but null: safe to assign, reset, swap, destroy or compare with nullptr; unsafe to dereference.

flashcards.front: Why prefer std::make_unique<T>(args...) over unique_ptr<T>(new T(args...))?
flashcards.back: No naked new, and exception-safe composition with other function arguments (no leak window between new and the wrapper taking ownership). C++14 onwards.
No, the raw-pointer constructor is explicit. Use make_unique or brace-init: std::unique_ptr<Fill> f{new Fill(3)};
